title: Harun al-Rashid and the Merchant of Oman

full_text:
Abu Hasan, a noble merchant of Oman, possessed a great fleet of trading ships that sailed the Indian Ocean. A catastrophic series of typhoons sank his vessels, and dishonest agents plundered his warehouses, reducing him from prince-like wealth to absolute poverty.

Refusing to default on his commercial obligations, Abu Hasan sold his palaces, his gardens, and his family heirlooms to pay every single dirham owed to his creditors, departing his native city with clean hands and a clear conscience.

Arriving in Baghdad, he took service as an assistant clerk in the imperial docks.

One evening, Caliph Harun al-Rashid, walking disguised through the harbor, observed Abu Hasan settling an intricate dispute between foreign sea captains with remarkable legal acumen, multilingual fluency, and unshakeable fairness.

The Caliph summoned the clerk to the imperial palace the next morning: 'Who are you, stranger, whose manners belong to a prince though your coat is frayed?'

Abu Hasan recounted the loss of his merchant fleet and his sacrifice to preserve his commercial honor without cheating a single creditor.

Harun al-Rashid stood from his throne, embraced the merchant, and declared before his ministers: 'A man who preserves his integrity when his empire collapses is richer than a king!'

The Caliph restored Abu Hasan’s fleet with twelve newly built merchant vessels from the royal shipyards of Basra, appointed him Admiral of the Commercial Fleets of the Caliphate, and granted him an estate in Baghdad, proving that honor tested by adversity receives the highest crown of restoration.
moral: Patient endurance under misfortune and fidelity to commercial honor receive imperial restoration.
